name: Clinical genetics and genetic counselling
summary: How expats access clinical genetics and genetic counselling in Singapore for hereditary cancer, carrier screening, rare disease workups, and prenatal questions — including consent, insurance, and cross-border report pitfalls.
body:
Genetic testing ads outrun genetic counselling. Clinical genetics services interpret whether a test should be ordered, what variants mean for relatives, and how results change screening — not just whether a spit-kit returns a colourful risk score.

## Common expat triggers
- Strong family cancer history (breast, ovarian, colorectal, prostate clusters)
- Carrier screening before or during pregnancy for known founder variants
- Child developmental or rare-disease odysseys after overseas inconclusive tests
- Pharmacogenetic curiosity — often oversold relative to clinical utility
- Reinterpreting DTC or foreign lab PDFs in a Singapore care context

## Counselling before kits
Pre-test counselling covers incidental findings, insurance implications, and who else in the family may need cascade testing. Post-test counselling translates VUS (variants of uncertain significance) into action or watchful waiting — a VUS is not a diagnosis.

## Access
Public hospital genetics services are referral-gated and high-value for complex cases. Private genetic counsellors and specialist clinics offer faster appointments; verify credentials and laboratory accreditation. Prenatal genetics often coordinates with O&G and fetal medicine.

## How to choose
Prefer board-trained genetics professionals who will decline low-utility panels. Ask which lab, which gene list, and how reanalysis works in two years. Bring pedigree notes spanning countries and prior reports in English.

## Practical tip
Do not upload raw DTC files into random “interpretation” websites before a clinical consult — misread variants drive unnecessary surgery anxiety. If relocating mid-workup, request a transfer summary with variant nomenclature (HGVS) intact.
